name: Pattern 3: Adaptive Practice
title: Pattern 3: Adaptive Practice
answer: Adaptive practice is software that watches how a student answers and adjusts the next question, giving harder items after correct answers and easier ones after mistakes. It matters because it is one of the oldest and best evidenced uses of AI in schools, but practice scores can rise while real understanding stays flat, so teachers must keep AI practice separate from checks done without the tool.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: Adaptive practice is one of the earliest forms of AI in schools. The software tracks a student's answers and changes the difficulty of the next question, moving to harder items after a run of correct answers and easier ones after a run of mistakes. Programs such as Zearn for elementary math and Khan Academy for older grades work in this way. The problem it solves is matching practice to each student's current level without the teacher hand picking every item. The teacher's role is to read what the software learned and use it to regroup students the next day.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, students work through adaptive practice while the software adjusts question difficulty in real time. The teacher then reviews what the software recorded and uses that information to regroup students for the next day's instruction. The text gives a middle school math example: three days of adaptive practice followed by one short quiz on paper each week, with the teacher comparing the two. It names Zearn for elementary math and Khan Academy for older grades as programs that work this way. The text does not give separate grade band guidance beyond those two examples.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The evidence here is steadier than for most patterns. A review of 21 studies of AI in kindergarten through 12th grade math found a small positive effect, larger when the software acted as an intelligent tutor or adaptive system (Yi et al., 2024). A second review found that intelligent tutors helped K through 12 students in general, but that the advantage shrank when the comparison was other practice software rather than no software at all (Letourneau, 2025). For students with disabilities, a review of 29 studies found a medium sized effect (Zhang, 2024).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The weak spot is the space between practice and learning. Practice scores can rise while real understanding stays flat, especially when students can game the software or lean on hints. That is why the idea in Chapter 7 keeps AI practice separate from regular checks done without the tool. In a middle school math class, that might mean three days of adaptive practice and one short quiz on paper each week, with the teacher comparing the two. The decisions about regrouping students and judging real understanding stay with the teacher.
